name: Ukraine
who: Russia vs Ukraine, with the US mediating talks
what: Full-scale invasion, now a grinding war of attrition
when: Started Feb 24, 2022 — day 1,650+ and still going
how: Daily drone, missile and artillery strikes along a front over 1,100 km long
current: Now in its fifth year with no sign of ending. Ukraine’s General Staff reported roughly 240 combat engagements a day in early September 2026. Trump envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner visited both Moscow and Kyiv in early September for direct talks, and Zelensky says he hopes for a trilateral US-Russia-Ukraine meeting "this fall." A three-day pause meant to allow that US visit ended with renewed Russian missile and drone strikes on Kyiv. Zelensky says Putin may also order a fresh mobilization of 300,000 troops after Russia’s September elections. No ceasefire or territorial deal has been reached.

name: Gaza
what: War technically under ceasefire, but violence continues
when: War since Oct 7, 2023; ceasefire since Oct 10, 2025
how: Over 1,300 people killed since the "ceasefire" began; disarmament and reconstruction stalled
current: A US-brokered ceasefire took effect Oct 10, 2025, built around Trump’s 20-point plan, but "ceasefire" has been a loose description of the reality on the ground. Gaza’s health ministry puts the death toll since October 2023 at 73,651 as of early September 2026, with over 1,300 of those killed since the truce began — including a botched Israeli special-forces raid on September 1 that set off an exchange of fire and airstrikes killing several Palestinians in Gaza City. Hamas’s disarmament, deployment of an international stabilization force, and reconstruction have all stalled.

name: Iran
who: Israel and the US vs Iran
what: A leadership-shattering war, now in an uneasy pause
how: US-Israeli strikes killed Iran’s Supreme Leader; his son succeeded him; Hormuz still shut
current: This escalated far beyond the original June 2025 war. On February 28, 2026, Israel and the US launched a major surprise air campaign on Iran — reported by multiple outlets as "Operation Epic Fury" — that killed Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei, 86, in Tehran, along with other senior officials. Iran’s Assembly of Experts named his son, Mojtaba Khamenei, as the new Supreme Leader on March 9, 2026, after a Pakistan-mediated ceasefire took hold in early April. That ceasefire has since frayed repeatedly, with Israel’s defense minister saying the military is ready to strike again "with even greater force" and Iran keeping the Strait of Hormuz effectively closed. Diplomats met at the UN General Assembly sidelines in late September 2026 without a breakthrough.

name: Sudan
who: Army (SAF) vs the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces
what: Civil war hardening into a formal partition
when: Since April 15, 2023, now in its 4th year
how: RSF controls Darfur and the west; army holds the center, north and east
current: The war has hardened into something close to a formal partition. RSF commander Mohamed Hamdan "Hemedti" Dagalo was formally sworn in around September 1, 2026, as head of a 31-member parallel "Tasis" government based in Nyala, with SPLM-N leader Abdel Aziz al-Hilu as his deputy and eight new regional governors installed. Meanwhile the army-backed government has retaken central and eastern Sudan and operates from Port Sudan. The siege of El-Fasher, Darfur’s historic capital, has now lasted more than 500 days; UNICEF says over 1,000 children have been killed or maimed by air, artillery and ground attacks. Drone warfare has intensified on both sides amid what aid groups call the world’s worst humanitarian crisis.

name: Sahel (Mali)
who: Al-Qaeda-linked JNIM and allied fighters vs the military government
what: Jihadist fuel blockade and insurgency threatening the junta
when: Blockade of the capital began around September 2025
how: Fuel convoys attacked, schools and businesses paralyzed; blockade has since eased somewhat
current: JNIM, al-Qaeda’s regional affiliate, imposed a fuel blockade on the capital Bamako beginning around September 2025 by attacking tanker convoys from Senegal and Ivory Coast — triggering months of fuel shortages, school closures and economic paralysis that analysts called the "toughest crisis" the junta has faced since seizing power in 2021. The blockade eased somewhat through 2026, but JNIM remains active within about 30 miles of the capital, and the broader insurgency continues to expand across the wider Sahel and into coastal West Africa.

name: Myanmar
who: Military junta vs resistance fighters and ethnic armed groups
what: Civil war following the 2021 coup, now with a civilian facade
when: Coup Feb 1, 2021; Min Aung Hlaing elected president April 3, 2026
how: Junta-backed party swept a sham election; war with resistance forces continues in the borderlands
current: Junta chief Min Aung Hlaing was elected president by a military-stacked parliament on April 3, 2026 (429 votes to 126), formalizing five years of army rule behind a civilian facade. This followed elections in December 2025 and January 2026 that the UN and Western governments dismissed as a sham, since Aung San Suu Kyi’s party was dissolved and major opposition groups didn’t contest. The civil war between the military and an alliance of ethnic armed organizations and pro-democracy resistance forces continues across large parts of the country’s borderlands.

name: Venezuela
who: US military vs Maduro; now a US-backed government vs the opposition
what: Maduro captured in a US raid, transition still in limbo
when: Raid on Jan 3, 2026; still no election date set
how: Acting president installed with US backing; opposition leader repeatedly blocked from returning
current: US special forces captured Nicolás Maduro and his wife Cilia Flores on January 3, 2026, flying them to the US to face narco-terrorism charges. US-backed Delcy Rodríguez has served as acting president since, well past the 180-day constitutional limit for an acting government (which technically expired around July 3). Twin earthquakes on June 24, 2026 compounded the humanitarian situation and became a political flashpoint, with opposition leader María Corina Machado citing the disaster response to press her case to return. At the UN General Assembly on September 22, 2026, Trump met Rodríguez face to face for the first time since the raid — the same day Machado made three separate failed attempts, by sea and air, to re-enter Venezuela from Panama, the seventh set of failed attempts since she left the country.

name: E. DR Congo
who: Rwanda-backed M23 vs the Congolese government
what: Peace deals signed, but M23 still controls the ground
when: Washington and Doha deals signed mid-2025; conflict decades old
how: M23 still controls Goma and Bukavu despite the agreements
current: A US-brokered framework between DR Congo and Rwanda was signed in Washington in mid-2025, alongside a separate Doha ceasefire between Kinshasa and the M23 rebel group. But a year after M23 seized Goma, the Rwanda-backed rebels still control the city and much of North and South Kivu province. DRC’s government has accused Rwanda of enabling "governance by crime" in the areas M23 controls, while the rebel alliance says it’s fighting for reform, not acting as a proxy force.

name: Taiwan Strait
who: China (PLA) vs Taiwan, with the US and Japan backing Taipei
what: Escalating military pressure just short of open conflict
how: Record Chinese aircraft and ship incursions into Taiwan’s air defense zone
current: China flew a record 2,076 sorties into Taiwan’s air defense identification zone through the year, Taiwan’s defense minister said — a pace so intense it complicates distinguishing routine drills from preparation for war. Taiwan has deployed HIMARS and put M1A2T Abrams tanks through combat-readiness drills, and President Lai has reiterated Taiwan’s "self-defense resolve," accusing Beijing of altering the regional status quo. Beijing has reportedly set 2027 as a rough internal benchmark for a credible invasion capability, though analysts are divided on whether that timeline is realistic, and there’s no current evidence an invasion is imminent.

current: North Korea has kept up a steady cadence of missile tests through 2026, including a tactical-nuclear-capable short-range ballistic missile test in June that state media said could inflict "fatal damage" on South Korean airfields, ports and power stations. Its first launch of the year came hours after the US raid that captured Maduro in Venezuela — a "decapitation" scenario North Korean leadership has long feared for itself. Pyongyang continues to reject Seoul’s dialogue overtures, formally calling the South a "hostile enemy state."

current: Confrontations between China’s coast guard and Philippine vessels escalated through 2026, including water-cannon attacks near Scarborough Shoal on consecutive days in late July and a Filipino sailor injured by a baton strike at Second Thomas Shoal. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio called Beijing’s actions "disturbing" and reaffirmed defense-treaty support for Manila. Japan sent combat troops to the annual Balikatan exercises with the Philippines for the first time since 1945.

name: Kashmir
what: Their worst clash in decades, now a fragile truce
how: Missile, drone and artillery exchange; US-mediated ceasefire holds, dispute unresolved
current: A ceasefire has held, if unevenly, since May 10, 2025, when a US-brokered truce ended the worst fighting between the two nuclear-armed neighbors in decades. The crisis began with an April 2025 attack on tourists in Indian Kashmir that killed 26 people, which India blamed on Pakistan-linked militants; days of missile, drone and artillery exchanges followed before Trump announced the ceasefire. Trade suspensions, visa cancellations and the suspension of the Indus Waters Treaty have all remained in place since, and the underlying Kashmir dispute remains unresolved.

name: Caucasus
what: Preliminary peace signed, but a final treaty remains unsigned
when: Framework signed Aug 8, 2025; still unresolved in 2026
how: Azerbaijan wants an Armenian constitutional change before signing a final deal
current: A preliminary peace framework, including the US-run TRIPP transit corridor linking Azerbaijan to its Nakhchivan exclave, was signed at the White House on August 8, 2025. But over a year later, a final peace treaty remains unsigned: Azerbaijan is insisting Armenia amend its constitution to explicitly recognize Baku’s sovereignty over Nagorno-Karabakh before it will sign, and there’s no indication a signing ceremony is imminent — even as both sides describe relations as "real peace" and TRIPP construction moves forward.

name: Thai–Cambodia border
what: Long-running border dispute that turned into open war twice in 2025
how: Artillery, tanks, drones and jets; 100+ killed before the latest ceasefire
current: What began as a five-day border clash in July 2025 reignited into the worst fighting between the two countries in years that December — three weeks of artillery, tank, drone and jet strikes that killed more than 100 people and displaced roughly a million civilians on both sides. A new ceasefire, with 16 de-escalation commitments, took hold on December 27, 2025, and has held since, though the underlying century-old border dispute remains unresolved.

name: Horn of Africa
what: Troop buildups and real border clashes amid fears of wider war
when: Tensions escalated sharply from early 2026; clashes in August
how: Ethiopian troops clashed with Tigrayan forces near the Eritrea-Sudan border triangle
current: Ethiopia and Eritrea moved troops toward their shared border in early 2026 amid what the International Crisis Group called a regional "powder keg," with Addis Ababa citing Red Sea port access as a "matter of survival" and each side accusing the other of arming rebel groups. Real fighting has already occurred: Ethiopian federal forces clashed with Tigrayan forces near the Ethiopia-Eritrea-Sudan border triangle in early August 2026, using artillery and drones. Still, a UN peacekeeping force commander said in late September there were no signs Eritrea itself was mobilizing for a new war, even as an exiled Eritrean opposition figure alleged otherwise — a reminder that the picture remains genuinely contested, not a settled march to war.
